The National Geographic Kids homepage was built like a toy: a pair of binoculars kids could look through, with the magazine’s franchises — Back Talk, What in the World?, Wild & Wacky and more — rebuilt as things to type into, unscramble, and print. Oddtoe designed and animated that homepage and a dozen of the interactive modules behind it. [/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Oddtoe ran the digital side of National Geographic Kids — online editor, designer, and cartoonist in one — and produced the award-winning site’s interactive homepage — the binocular navigation above — and designed its games and content for nearly six years: a rolling immersive feature in layered parallax, plus the game modules that turned magazine pages into play — caption tools, photo puzzles, fill-in stories, and quiz engines the editorial team could refill themselves.

Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries.

How do you move a kids’ magazine onto a screen?

[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Not by scanning the pages. A nine-year-old opens a website the way they open a toy box — so the homepage became a pair of binoculars, the subscribe card a magazine cover that flips, and every franchise from the printed magazine became something to do rather than something to read.

The brief had a second audience: the editors. A game that needs a developer for every new issue dies after three issues. So the modules were built as refillable engines — the fill-in stories read from a plain text file, the quizzes from an XML file — and the monthly immersive feature ran on a repeatable layered template. The magazine could keep the site as fresh as the print run without rebuilding anything.

How did the immersive homepage feature work?

[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

The homepage carried a rolling immersive feature: a 738×330 scene built in three animated layers — foreground, middleground, background — so an underwater world or a wolf pack had depth kids could feel. Each edition was a fresh scene composed on the same layered template.

The template is the quiet hero. Because every scene decomposed into the same three layers, a new edition meant new artwork, not new engineering — the design rounds in the archive move from underwater scenes to wolves to outer space on one production system. It is the same character-and-world thinking Oddtoe now sells as character design services for brands.

The immersive feature — running here, live, in a Flash emulator: an underwater world painted in three layers behind the welcome banner, with the photo rail racked underneath — sea lions in the middleground, the foreground waiting for a click. It never begged for attention — it made the page feel inhabited, the way a good toy shop window does. That restraint is a design position: motion sells the world, the words sell the click.

What does this project say about Oddtoe now?

[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Everything on this page is character design plus systems thinking: mascots with personality, worlds with depth, and engines an editorial team could drive without a developer. That combination — not any single game — is the deliverable.

It is also the through-line to the studio’s current work. The layered scenes and refillable engines have become generative AI animation pipelines; the mascots and side characters have become character design services; and the instinct that a screen should be a toy runs straight into Oddtoe’s brand activations for venues and events.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]

What the playable magazine did

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Play was the strategy, not the reward. While Oddtoe ran the site’s digital side, the audience — and the magazine behind it — grew with it.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="30" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="30"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="2/3"][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/6"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="" dfd_enable_overlay="" el_id="pat-faq"][vc_column width="1/4"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/2"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][vc_column_text css="" item_animation="transition.fadeIn"]

Questions & Answers

The National Geographic Kids work

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_accordion style="style-3" active_section="1" font_size="18" tab_title_google_fonts="yes" tab_title_custom_fonts="font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal" icon_size="14"][vc_tta_section title="What did Oddtoe actually build for National Geographic Kids?" tab_id="1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

The interactive homepage — the binocular navigation — plus the rolling immersive homepage feature in three animated layers, and a lineup of game modules: Back Talk (caption and print), What in the World? (photo anagrams), Wild & Wacky (fill-in stories), quiz engines, character e-cards, and promotional builds including a WordGirl crossover with PBS.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Are the images on this page mock-ups?" tab_id="1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

No. They are the original builds captured live in a Flash emulator — the animated frames show the real modules running, including a fill-in story completed end to end.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How could the magazine update the games without a developer?" tab_id="1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

The engines were refillable: fill-in stories read from a plain text file, quizzes from an XML file, and the monthly immersive feature ran on a repeatable three-layer template. New issue, new content, same engines.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What made the homepage design work for kids?" tab_id="1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

It behaved like a toy. Navigation lived inside a pair of binoculars, franchises were verbs — type, unscramble, fill in, rate — and motion was used to make the page feel inhabited rather than to shout. Every module still pointed back to the printed magazine.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Does Oddtoe still do this kind of work?" tab_id="1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0"][vc_column_text css=""]

Yes — the same skills, with a modern pipeline. Character and mascot work runs through character design services; layered scene-building now runs through generative AI animation; and playable-first thinking drives the studio’s experiential and brand-activation projects. Start with the enquiry form on this page.

The pig, the balloon, and the print button

[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="19"][vc_column_text css=""]

The clearest statement of the whole project is Back Talk. A real photograph — a pig staring into an open fridge — and one empty thought balloon with the words TYPE HERE! The kid supplies the joke, and the punchline of the interface is the button underneath: PRINT.

That print button is doing serious work. It turns a web page into a thing a kid makes and takes away — onto the fridge, into the classroom, next to the magazine it came from. The interactive is not competing with print; it is feeding it.

Each franchise got the same treatment: find the one verb a kid wants to do, and build the whole screen around it. What in the World? is unscramble. Wild & Wacky is fill in the blanks — fifteen of them, rewarded with an illustrated story starring whatever the kid typed. The quizzes are rate yourself, with ranks like “Supreme Sea Monster” doing the encouragement.

One verb per screen is still how Oddtoe starts an interactive brief, whether the audience is nine or thirty-nine. It is the fastest way to find out whether an idea is an experience or just a layout — and it is the thinking behind the studio’s brand activation work today.

Where the characters came from

[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="19"][vc_column_text css=""]

Before and alongside the National Geographic Kids work, Oddtoe was drawing its own characters — the Parasite Island cast and the illustrated portfolio the studio was built on.

Those characters carried into the magazine work: the quiz engine’s logo is a cartoon toe — the studio’s namesake — and original characters run through the games, e-cards and homepage scenes. Oddtoe also drew a comic strip that ran in the printed magazine — a story this site will tell in its own case study.

Characters built for kids have to survive rough handling. They get printed badly, animated at small sizes, and judged in half a second. Designing under those constraints is a discipline, and it is the reason the studio’s character design services start with silhouette and personality before style.

The archive behind this case study — the layered scenes, the engines, the cast — is also the seedbed for Oddtoe’s own stories, now made with a generative AI animation pipeline the original Flash toolkit could only dream about. Same instinct, faster hands.

The National Geographic Kids homepage was built like a toy: a pair of binoculars kids could look through, with the magazine’s franchises — Back Talk, What in the World?, Wild & Wacky and more — rebuilt as things to type into, unscramble, and print. Oddtoe designed and animated that homepage and a dozen of the interactive modules behind it. Every image on this page is the real work, running again — starting with the homepage itself: click the five markers to read it the way a nine-year-old did, region by region.

[/vc_column_text]

The project in one paragraph

What did Oddtoe make for National Geographic Kids?

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

Oddtoe ran the digital side of National Geographic Kids — online editor, designer, and cartoonist in one — and produced the award-winning site’s interactive homepage — the binocular navigation above — and designed its games and content for nearly six years: a rolling immersive feature in layered parallax, plus the game modules that turned magazine pages into play — caption tools, photo puzzles, fill-in stories, and quiz engines the editorial team could refill themselves.

Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries.

Everything hung off one front door

One homepage, twelve builds

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

The hub is the binocular homepage — the site’s playful front door. Around it, the twelve interactive builds Oddtoe designed for National Geographic Kids: the games and puzzles kids played, the monthly immersive scene, the characters, and the promos that pointed back to print.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

The design problem

How do you move a kids’ magazine onto a screen?

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

Not by scanning the pages. A nine-year-old opens a website the way they open a toy box — so the homepage became a pair of binoculars, the subscribe card a magazine cover that flips, and every franchise from the printed magazine became something to do rather than something to read.

The brief had a second audience: the editors. A game that needs a developer for every new issue dies after three issues. So the modules were built as refillable engines — the fill-in stories read from a plain text file, the quizzes from an XML file — and the monthly immersive feature ran on a repeatable layered template. The magazine could keep the site as fresh as the print run without rebuilding anything.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”full_width_content_paddings” el_id=”pat-section-1″][vc_column]

A scene, not a banner

How did the immersive homepage feature work?

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

The homepage carried a rolling immersive feature: a 738×330 scene built in three animated layers — foreground, middleground, background — so an underwater world or a wolf pack had depth kids could feel. Each edition was a fresh scene composed on the same layered template.

The template is the quiet hero. Because every scene decomposed into the same three layers, a new edition meant new artwork, not new engineering — the design rounds in the archive move from underwater scenes to wolves to outer space on one production system. It is the same character-and-world thinking Oddtoe now sells as character design services for brands.

[/vc_column_text]

The immersive feature — running here, live, in a Flash emulator: an underwater world painted in three layers behind the welcome banner, with the photo rail racked underneath — sea lions in the middleground, the foreground waiting for a click. It never begged for attention — it made the page feel inhabited, the way a good toy shop window does. That restraint is a design position: motion sells the world, the words sell the click.

Character work, engine work

What does this project say about Oddtoe now?

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

Everything on this page is character design plus systems thinking: mascots with personality, worlds with depth, and engines an editorial team could drive without a developer. That combination — not any single game — is the deliverable.

It is also the through-line to the studio’s current work. The layered scenes and refillable engines have become generative AI animation pipelines; the mascots and side characters have become character design services; and the instinct that a screen should be a toy runs straight into Oddtoe’s brand activations for venues and events.

[/vc_column_text]

Questions & Answers

The National Geographic Kids work

[/vc_column_text]

[dfd_accordion style=”style-3″ active_section=”1″ font_size=”18″ tab_title_google_fonts=”yes” tab_title_custom_fonts=”font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal” icon_size=”14″][vc_tta_section title=”What did Oddtoe actually build for National Geographic Kids?” tab_id=”1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

The interactive homepage — the binocular navigation — plus the rolling immersive homepage feature in three animated layers, and a lineup of game modules: Back Talk (caption and print), What in the World? (photo anagrams), Wild & Wacky (fill-in stories), quiz engines, character e-cards, and promotional builds including a WordGirl crossover with PBS.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Are the images on this page mock-ups?” tab_id=”1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

No. They are the original builds captured live in a Flash emulator — the animated frames show the real modules running, including a fill-in story completed end to end.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”How could the magazine update the games without a developer?” tab_id=”1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

The engines were refillable: fill-in stories read from a plain text file, quizzes from an XML file, and the monthly immersive feature ran on a repeatable three-layer template. New issue, new content, same engines.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What made the homepage design work for kids?” tab_id=”1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

It behaved like a toy. Navigation lived inside a pair of binoculars, franchises were verbs — type, unscramble, fill in, rate — and motion was used to make the page feel inhabited rather than to shout. Every module still pointed back to the printed magazine.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Does Oddtoe still do this kind of work?” tab_id=”1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0″][vc_column_text css=””]

Yes — the same skills, with a modern pipeline. Character and mascot work runs through character design services; layered scene-building now runs through generative AI animation; and playable-first thinking drives the studio’s experiential and brand-activation projects. Start with the enquiry form on this page.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][/dfd_accordion][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”” el_id=”pat-article-1″][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”4/6″]

Verbs, not pages

The pig, the balloon, and the print button

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

The clearest statement of the whole project is Back Talk. A real photograph — a pig staring into an open fridge — and one empty thought balloon with the words TYPE HERE! The kid supplies the joke, and the punchline of the interface is the button underneath: PRINT.

That print button is doing serious work. It turns a web page into a thing a kid makes and takes away — onto the fridge, into the classroom, next to the magazine it came from. The interactive is not competing with print; it is feeding it.

Each franchise got the same treatment: find the one verb a kid wants to do, and build the whole screen around it. What in the World? is unscramble. Wild & Wacky is fill in the blanks — fifteen of them, rewarded with an illustrated story starring whatever the kid typed. The quizzes are rate yourself, with ranks like “Supreme Sea Monster” doing the encouragement.

One verb per screen is still how Oddtoe starts an interactive brief, whether the audience is nine or thirty-nine. It is the fastest way to find out whether an idea is an experience or just a layout — and it is the thinking behind the studio’s brand activation work today.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”” dfd_enable_overlay=”” el_class=”ngk-quote-row”][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”2/3″][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″][vc_single_image image=”16226″ img_size=”medium” alignment=”center” style=”vc_box_shadow_3d” onclick=”link_image” css=””][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″]
This is really when Oddtoe took off. Comic strips, game design, interactive storytelling — all at National Geographic. Loved it.

Oddtoe

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”” el_id=”pat-article-2″][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”4/6″]

From flea circus to front page

Where the characters came from

[vc_column_text css=””]

[/vc_column_text]

[vc_column_text css=””]

Before and alongside the National Geographic Kids work, Oddtoe was drawing its own characters — the Parasite Island cast and the illustrated portfolio the studio was built on.

Those characters carried into the magazine work: the quiz engine’s logo is a cartoon toe — the studio’s namesake — and original characters run through the games, e-cards and homepage scenes. Oddtoe also drew a comic strip that ran in the printed magazine — a story this site will tell in its own case study.

Characters built for kids have to survive rough handling. They get printed badly, animated at small sizes, and judged in half a second. Designing under those constraints is a discipline, and it is the reason the studio’s character design services start with silhouette and personality before style.

The archive behind this case study — the layered scenes, the engines, the cast — is also the seedbed for Oddtoe’s own stories, now made with a generative AI animation pipeline the original Flash toolkit could only dream about. Same instinct, faster hands.

[/vc_column_text]
